Presents the behavioural explanation fairly: smoking, diet, alcohol and inactivity are socially patterned
Critiques it with Whitehall (behaviour explains only part of the gradient) and Black Report materialist view
Shows structure shapes 'choice': income, housing, food environments, stress, education, life course
Considers psychosocial explanations (control, status; Wilkinson and Pickett, noting debate)
Considers healthcare's role (inverse care law) and selection/reverse causation
Implications for doctors and policy (proportionate universalism, Core20PLUS5, social prescribing)
Clear structure and a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Health inequalities are systematic differences in health between social groups; Whitehead called those that are avoidable and unfair health inequities. In England, life expectancy and healthy life expectancy fall at each step down the deprivation scale. The claim that this is mainly due to lifestyle has some support. Smoking, poor diet, heavy drinking and inactivity are more common in deprived groups and cause much of the excess in heart disease and lung cancer.

However, three lines of evidence suggest lifestyle is only part of the story. First, the Whitehall studies of civil servants found a steep mortality gradient by employment grade, and conventional risk factors explained only part of it. Second, the Black Report (1980) argued that material and structural conditions such as income, housing and working conditions were the most important explanations. Third, 'choice' is itself socially shaped. Cheap energy-dense food, the density of fast-food outlets and off-licences, chronic stress, insecure work and low educational opportunity all make healthy behaviour harder. Dahlgren and Whitehead's model places lifestyle within layers of social and economic conditions, and life-course research shows that disadvantage builds up from before birth.

Psychosocial explanations add a further layer: low control and low status may harm health directly through stress pathways, and Wilkinson and Pickett argue that unequal societies do worse overall, though this is debated. Selection also plays some role, because illness can push people down the income scale. Finally, healthcare can widen gaps: Tudor Hart's inverse care law describes good care being least available where need is greatest.

For doctors, a lifestyle-only view risks victim-blaming and stigmatising language. A better response combines individual support (such as stopping smoking) with attention to social circumstances, social prescribing, outreach, and advocacy for policies following Marmot's proportionate universalism. I conclude that lifestyle is an important pathway through which social conditions affect health, but not the main cause: behaviour and structure are intertwined, and structural conditions largely explain why behaviours differ.

questions.q: Ethics essay: 'Respect for patient autonomy means doctors must always give patients what they ask for.' Discuss with reference to law and ethical argument in England and Wales.
markScheme: Defines autonomy (thin vs rich; relational) and its grounding (Kant, Mill)
Distinguishes negative right to refuse from positive right to demand treatment
Law on refusal: competent adults may refuse (Re T; MCA s1(4) unwise decisions); valid consent elements
Law on demands: no right to demand treatment the clinician considers inappropriate (e.g. Burke v GMC 2005, Aintree v James); Montgomery requires information about reasonable alternatives
Competing principles: beneficence, non-maleficence, justice/resource limits, professional integrity
Limits of autonomy: capacity, children (Gillick, Re W), harm to others
Shared decision-making as reconciling autonomy and expertise
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Respect for autonomy means respecting a person's capacity to govern their own life according to their own values. Kant grounds it in the dignity of rational agents, who should never be treated merely as means; Mill grounds it in the claim that individuals are the best judges of their own good, so power may be used against their will only to prevent harm to others. On a thin view, autonomy is a right to non-interference; on a richer view, autonomous choices are informed and reflective, made within relationships.

The key distinction is between refusing and demanding. English law strongly protects refusal: a competent adult may refuse treatment for rational, irrational or no reasons, even if death results (Re T, 1993), and the Mental Capacity Act 2005 states that an unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity. Montgomery (2015) further requires doctors to disclose material risks and reasonable alternatives, so that patients can choose among options.

But there is no equivalent right to demand treatment. In R (Burke) v GMC (2005) the Court of Appeal held that a doctor is not obliged to provide treatment they consider clinically inappropriate, and in Aintree v James (2013) the Supreme Court said patients cannot demand treatment that is not clinically indicated. Ethically this is justified on several grounds. Beneficence and non-maleficence mean a doctor should not harm the patient, for example by prescribing antibiotics for a viral illness. Justice means resources such as expensive drugs or ICU beds must be shared fairly, and antibiotic resistance harms others. And professional integrity means doctors are not mere instruments of patient preference. Autonomy also has preconditions: capacity, adequate information and voluntariness. For children, the law gives weight to Gillick-competent consent but allows refusals to be overridden (Re W).

This does not reduce autonomy to the right to say no. Shared decision-making asks doctors to present the reasonable options and help patients choose among them in light of their values. I conclude that respect for autonomy requires doctors to respect refusals and to give patients genuine choice among appropriate options, but not to supply whatever is requested.
